newsitem.title: MALDIVES: Incongruous scenes at paradise summit.
newsitem.headline: Incongruous scenes at paradise summit.

text.p: The leaders of India and Pakistan on Monday held their first face-to-face talks at a beach resort where the cost of a two-night stay exceeds India's annual per capita income.
They then held a news conference in an open-air discotheque, with a bar and a swimming pool as the backdrop.

The site of the talks between Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, was only part of the incongruous tableau on display at the summit of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).
Heads of state and government travel between islands in this sun-drenched archipelago in powerful speed boats accompanied by armed guards.
At the Kurumba Village Resort, the leaders of the seven SAARC member states wear formal dress while vacationers frolic nearby in bathing suits.

Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga strolls by the pool in full sari, surrounded by aides and bodyguards, while women in bikinis lounge nearby. A sign at the entrance reads: "Nudism is prohibited."
Like other holiday paradises in the Maldives, Kurumba is an island unto itself with 177 rooms in beachside bungalows that hug the emerald waters of the Indian Ocean.

About half the resort has been taken up by the leaders of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka for a three-day summit which started on Monday, leaving the rest to any Robinson Crusoe able to pay some $180 a night per double room.
India's annual per capita income is about $280, while Pakistan's is some $500.
The resort's brochure calls it a "fun lover's island". But it is not all frivolity. A lime soda at the Palm Bar costs $6.05 -- invoiced in U.S. dollars and including service charge.
It was in the discotheque at the end of the bar where Gujral and Sharif held the news conference after 90 minutes of talks.

Reporters stood on the octagonal wooden dance floor while the two leaders answered questions. Behind them, resort employees had draped yellow and red material over a screen and liquor bottles in the bar had been replaced by flowers.
